Mitigations are discussed in [section 6](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security#name-mitigating-against-cross-de). It might be useful to have a dedicated section about this topic. (in V2.7?)

"V5.7 Consent Management" is related to this. By ensuring the user consent this type of attack can be somewhat mitigated (but people don't read consent screens …). However, this topic/issue is more general that OAuth flows and it would be better if the requirements were in another chapter.

"V2.7 Out-of-Band authentication mechanisms" is what is the more appropriate, I think. however:

* This is not only for authentication but for delegated authorization as well. I think, this could still fit in this section.
* V2.7 seems to be currently about flows where a code is sent to the user to a third party device channel and must then be entered in the application (in the session). The alternative scenario where the user uses another application (eg. a mobile application) to authorize the access (and where the consumption device is not the same as the authorization device) is not really covered in the current requirements too much, I think.

> "device code phising"

Device code phishing seems to refer about OAUth [Device Code Grant](https://oauth.net/2/device-flow/) more specifically. Maybe a more general "cross-device fishing attack" could be used?

For reference, [draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security) talks about:

* Cross-Device *Consent* Phishing (CDCP) → fishing to get a delegated access (eg. access token);
* Cross-Device *Session* Phishing (CDSP)  → fishing to get a session.

> > This may for example include unique binding code (e.g. QR codes).
>
> What exactly it means? Who need to what with that?

We should be flexible in this regard. There are several (at least two) viable solutions for this (which are implemented in different protocols):

* When using **OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant**, the *AS* generates a unique code which is sent to the client, from there to the user, from there in the AS again (and the code can be embedded in a URL which can be transmitted to the user for example as a QR code).
* When using the **User Code Interaction of GNAP**, it works basically the same way AFAIU.
* When using **CIBA**, the *client* generates a binding message (code) which,
  1. is sent directly to the user (eg. through the client UI)
  2. is sent as well to the AS, from there to the user, and from there displayed to the user (eg. through push notification);
  3. the user is then expected to check that the two values match.
